one_liner: Research Python simulator of Cacheus (FAST'21), a learned two-expert page-cache eviction policy that competes with ARC/LIRS/DLIRS on hit rate.
what_it_does: A trace-driven cache simulator from the FAST'21 authors. It contains Cacheus plus 11 other policies (MIN, LRU, LFU, MRU, ARC, LIRS, DLIRS, LeCaR and three ALeCaR variants) and reports hit rate on block-I/O traces. run.py takes a JSON config listing traces, algorithms and cache sizes (as fractions of the trace footprint) and prints or appends CSV results. Each policy is a Python class, Cacheus(cache_size, window_size, **kwargs), whose request(key, ts) returns (CacheOp.HIT or INSERT, evicted_key). It tracks keys only and stores no values, so it is a policy model, not a usable cache container.
how_it_is_fast: The gain is hit rate, not speed. Following LeCaR, it uses online regret minimization: on each eviction it samples one of two experts by weight, and when a missed key is found in an expert's eviction history (each N/2 entries), that expert's weight is multiplied by exp(-learning_rate). Expert one is SR-LRU (scan-resistant LRU): the cache is split into a reuse partition R and a small scan-resistant partition SR that new keys enter, evictions come only from SR, and the partition sizes adapt when demoted or new items are re-referenced. Expert two is CR-LFU (churn-resistant LFU), an LFU heap that breaks frequency ties by evicting the most recently used key, which pins a stable subset during churn. The learning rate itself is tuned every N requests by stochastic hill climbing and resets after 10 degrading windows, so no hyperparameters are hand-set.
when_to_use: Reproducing the FAST'21 results, or using Cacheus as a baseline in cache-policy research on block-storage traces (FIU and MSR readers are built in)
Estimating, before any native implementation, whether a fixed-size page or block cache (buffer cache, SSD or flash cache tier) would gain hit rate from an adaptive recency/frequency policy
Workloads that shift between scan, churn, LRU-friendly and LFU-friendly phases, with caches small relative to footprint (the paper tests 0.05%-10%)
When you want LeCaR-style learned eviction without hand-tuning the learning or discount rate
As a readable reference to port; for reusable code, use libCacheSim's Apache-2.0 C port (Cacheus.c, SR_LRU.c, CR_LFU.c)
when_not_to_use: Any throughput- or latency-sensitive path: it is pure Python with an O(log N) LFU heap update on every hit and no concurrency, and no throughput numbers are published
Variable-size objects (web, CDN, key-value caches): the simulator counts unit-size 4 KiB pages and the cache size is in pages
Memory-constrained caches: the paper states about 2N metadata entries (N resident plus N history), and the SIEVE paper (NSDI'24) puts Cacheus per-object metadata at 3.3x LRU's

Workloads where most objects are requested exactly twice with a gap: the S3-FIFO paper (SOSP'23) names Cacheus among partitioned policies that handle this badly at small cache sizes, and found Cacheus often less competitive than traditional algorithms such as ARC in its broad simulations
Code reuse in products: the repo has no LICENSE file

integration.dependencies: numpy and matplotlib (matplotlib is imported at module level by the Visualizinator that every policy loads); no requirements file or packaging
integration.min_toolchain: Python 3 (README uses python3; exact version not documented)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; single-threaded simulator objects with no locking
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — within this simulator it exposes the same request(key, ts) interface as the repo's LRU class, so swapping is a config change; it holds no values and is not a drop-in for a real LRU cache

gotchas: Won't run out of the box: example.config is invalid JSON (trailing comma in the alecar6 block) and doesn't list cacheus, and run_alg.py still calls the constructor and request() with one argument, which raises TypeError for Cacheus

The code differs from the paper. It starts the learning rate deterministically at sqrt(2 ln 2 / N) rather than a random value in [0.001, 1], and the constructor calls np.random.seed(123), which resets numpy's global RNG for anything else in the process. libCacheSim's port says it follows the paper instead, so results from the two can differ.
Memory grows with trace length: the learning-rate updater appends to a list on every request, even with visualization turned off

SR-LRU and CR-LFU are not separate modules. They are inlined in cacheus.py (s = R, q = SR, and the heap's tie-break in Cacheus_Entry.__lt__). Open issue #16 (June 2025, no reply) asks where they are, so readers can mistake the code for plain LRU+LFU.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Cacheus over SIEVE, S3-FIFO and GL-Cache (all in libCacheSim, which also carries a Cacheus port) only when the target is a unit-size block or page storage cache with mixed scan and churn phases, and hit rate matters more than CPU and metadata cost. For throughput, simplicity or web/KV traces, use SIEVE or S3-FIFO. For a production in-process cache, use Caffeine or W-TinyLFU. For variable-size objects, use LHD, AdaptSize or LRB.
verified_claims_summary: Only simulated hit rate was measured, in Python, with no compiler, hardware or throughput numbers. The study ran 17,766 simulations on 329 one-day block-I/O traces from 5 datasets at 6 cache sizes (0.05%-10% of footprint). In paired t-tests over the paper's 30 workload/cache-size combinations, Cacheus C3 is distinctly best in 47%, indistinguishable from the best of ARC/LIRS/DLIRS/LeCaR in about 40%, and worse in 13%. The extremes are +38.32 absolute hit-rate points vs ARC (CloudPhysics, 10%) and -15.12 vs DLIRS (MSR, 5%). The paper gives no isolated Cacheus-vs-LRU number; LRU appears only in the compared set and the ranking study.
status_note: Stale research code: cacheus.py last changed in April 2021 (bug fixes) and the repo last changed in October 2023. With no LICENSE it is reference-only; the maintained, Apache-2.0 route is libCacheSim's C port (relicensed September 2026), though that port has open TODOs such as 'this function may not work' in Cacheus_to_evict.
